planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, calcareous, well-drained soil for natural winter stratification; this branching rosinweed is a narrow endemic of open limestone woodlands and outcrops on the southern Cumberland Plateau in Alabama, Georgia, and Tennessee.

directions: Direct sow in fall on lean, well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun and allow seeds to cold-stratify naturally over winter; germination follows the slow, taproot-first pattern typical of the genus, with flowering delayed until the second or third year. Cumberland Rosinweed gets its species name from its openly branched, candelabra-like flowering stems, which rise 3-6 feet and split repeatedly above mid-height before topping out in bright yellow, sunflower-like composite blooms through mid-to-late summer. It is a true regional rarity, restricted to open calcareous glades and rocky woodland edges across only a handful of counties spanning the Alabama-Georgia-Tennessee Cumberland Plateau, and its late-season flowers are an important nectar and pollen source for long-tongued native bees when many other prairie plants have finished blooming. Once its deep taproot is established the plant is extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived, but it resents any disturbance or transplanting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for winter stratification and spring emergence, or start indoors and transplant while young; the deep taproot resents disturbance once formed, so choose a permanent site.

directions: Sow in fall in gritty, well-drained glade or prairie soil in full sun, or start seed indoors and set out transplants while still small to avoid disturbing the taproot. Unlike its sprawling relative Callirhoe involucrata, Bush's Poppy Mallow grows as a more upright, self-supporting clump 1-2 feet tall and wide, bearing large magenta-pink, cup-shaped flowers from early summer into fall. It is native to limestone and dolomite glades and open rocky woodlands across Missouri, Arkansas, Kansas, and Oklahoma, and is considered critically imperiled through much of that range, making garden and restoration plantings valuable for regional conservation. Bees are frequent visitors to the showy flowers, and established plants tolerate heat and drought with ease once the deep taproot is set.

planting.note: Direct sow into loose, deep sandy soil in fall; this federally endangered species is restricted to deep sand deposits along the Colorado River in central Texas and requires excellent drainage.

directions: Direct sow into loose, deep, sandy soil in full sun in fall, giving seedlings a permanent spot since the thickened taproot does not transplant well once established. Texas Poppy Mallow is a tall, erect Callirhoe reaching 2-4 feet, producing large magenta-red cup-shaped flowers marked with a darker crimson eye at the base of each petal from late spring through summer. It survives today in only a handful of deep-sand populations along the Colorado River in central Texas and has been federally listed as endangered since 1981 due to habitat loss, so cultivated plantings from responsibly sourced seed play a real role in its conservation. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and best suited to sandy, well-drained gardens rather than heavier clay soils.

planting.note: Scarify or cold-stratify seed before fall direct sowing into lean, well-drained prairie soil; like other Dalea species it forms a deep taproot early and should not be transplanted.

directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into lean, well-drained prairie or hillside soil in full sun, allowing natural cold-moist stratification to break dormancy over winter. Nine-anther Prairie Clover forms one to a few erect, wiry stems that branch openly above the middle, with fine, gray-green pinnately compound foliage and two-ranked spikes of small white flowers that open from July into September, later than most of its purple- and white-flowered relatives. Native from the Dakotas and Montana south through the Great Plains to Texas and New Mexico, it is a nitrogen-fixing legume typically found on loess hill prairies and dry stream valleys, and its late-summer bloom period makes it a valuable nectar source for native bees when many other prairie legumes have finished flowering. It is slow to establish but long-lived and highly drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is set, and is rarely offered outside specialty native seed sources.
